claims.text: The initial equimolar HEA nanoparticles are single-phase crystalline solid solutions.
Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent metals increases lattice strain.
Elevated lattice strain facilitates local elemental clustering and segregation.
Local clustering and elemental segregation lead to eventual phase separation.
The size-mismatch-driven mechanism governs stability under catalytic and thermoelectric operation from 473 to 1923 K.
Metal substitution can create a controlled variation in atomic size mismatch while preserving equimolar ratios.
Higher-mismatch nanoparticles will begin to segregate or phase-separate earlier than lower-mismatch nanoparticles.
Higher-mismatch nanoparticles will exhibit more pronounced segregation or phase separation than lower-mismatch nanoparticles.
Increased lattice strain by itself can be treated as a sign of phase separation.
A baseline HEA selected to minimize atomic size differences remains a stable single-phase solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
The causal comparison can isolate atomic size mismatch while holding synthesis kinetics, metal loading, and operating conditions constant.
Phase-separation behavior may depend on element-specific interactions in addition to atomic size mismatch.
Temperature and annealing duration can affect whether an equimolar solid solution remains stable or decomposes.
In situ XRD can monitor lattice-parameter changes and detect phase separation in the proposed nanoparticles.
TEM-EDS mapping can identify local elemental segregation and clustering in the proposed nanoparticles.
High-resolution XRD or neutron diffraction can quantitatively measure lattice strain in the proposed nanoparticles.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in strain, clustering, segregation, or earlier phase separation in the higher-mismatch material would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions require identical annealing kinetics, whereas the mechanism predicts that size mismatch changes the onset of segregation and the uncertainty field explicitly states that phase-separation kinetics may vary. Identical annealing schedules could be imposed, but identical kinetics cannot simultaneously be assumed and tested.
